Your fingerprints are unlike anyone else's on the planet - not even identical twins share the same prints. From the moment you were born, your unique ridge patterns have been the most reliable way to identify you.
Welcome to Day 1 of the Chabot STEM Workshop! Today you will become a fingerprint analyst.

Today's Case Briefing:: A set of unidentified fingerprints was recovered from a crime scene. Your mission: learn the three major fingerprint pattern types - Loop, Whorl, and Arch - then use your new skills to classify prints and identify a suspect.

Use the Fingerprint Ridge Classifier to study the three pattern types. Explore the Reference Guide to learn identifying features, then test yourself in Quiz Mode.
Interactive App: Launch Fingerprint Ridge Classifier. Use the Launch button below to open the app inline.
Ink your fingertip: Press firmly onto the ink pad and roll from side to side.
Transfer to card: Press your inked finger onto the white card, rolling smoothly from one side to the other.
Examine your print: Use a magnifying glass to examine your print. Classify it as a Loop, Whorl, or Arch.
Repeat and record: Repeat for all ten fingers and record your results on the classification chart.

When a drop of blood hits a surface, its shape tells a story. Forensic scientists use physics to calculate exactly where it came from.
Welcome to Day 2! Today you will become a bloodstain pattern analyst.

Today's Case Briefing:: Investigators found blood drops at a scene, but they need to know the angle of impact to determine what happened. Your mission: use the relationship between drop shape and impact angle to reconstruct the event.

items.text: I read the case briefing and watched the blood spatter video

blocks.content: Woven notebook: open your notebook now. As you move through this phase, write your answers to every reflection, discussion, and case-study question before moving on. Your notebook is the record of your thinking.
Materials Needed: Washable red paint, Pipettes, Protractors, Rulers, Butcher paper, Smocks or old shirts, Calculators, Tablets for the app
Use the Blood Spatter Angle Calculator to understand how drop width and length determine impact angle. Try the Calculator tab first, then challenge yourself in Practice Mode.
Interactive App: Launch Spatter Angle Calculator. Use the Launch button below to open the app inline.
Prepare workspace: Put on your smock and cover your workspace with butcher paper.
Vertical drop test: Using the pipette, release a single drop of simulated blood from 30 cm directly above the paper. Measure the resulting circle.
Angled drop test: Tilt a clean sheet of butcher paper to 45 degrees. Release a drop and measure the resulting ellipse (width and length).
Calculate impact angle: Calculate the impact angle using the formula: angle = arcsin(width / length).
Multiple angles: Repeat at different angles (30, 60, 75 degrees) and record all results.

Your heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day. Each beat creates an electrical signal that tells doctors exactly what is happening inside your chest.
Welcome to Day 5! Today you step into Mini Med School as a clinical technician.
Today's Case Briefing:: A patient arrives with an abnormal heart rhythm. Your mission: learn to measure vital signs, interpret EKG waveforms, and determine what rhythm the patient is in.

items.text: I read the case briefing and watched the vital signs video

blocks.content: Woven notebook: open your notebook now. As you move through this phase, write your answers to every reflection, discussion, and case-study question before moving on. Your notebook is the record of your thinking.
Materials Needed: Stethoscopes, Blood pressure cuffs, Pulse oximeters, Stopwatches, Vital signs sheets, Tablets for the app

Use the EKG Waveform Explorer to study 5 different cardiac rhythms. Explore Normal Sinus Rhythm first, then compare it to Tachycardia, Bradycardia, AFib, and STEMI. When you feel ready, test yourself in Quiz Mode.
Interactive App: Launch EKG Waveform Explorer. Use the Launch button below to open the app inline.
Measure heart rate: Find your radial pulse (wrist) and count beats for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4 for your heart rate.
Measure oxygen saturation: Use the pulse oximeter to measure your oxygen saturation (SpO2). Record the number.
Measure blood pressure: Practice taking a blood pressure reading with the cuff and stethoscope. Record systolic and diastolic values.
Exercise and retest: Do 20 jumping jacks, then immediately re-measure your heart rate and SpO2. Compare to your resting values.
